overview: The atlas label Papuan is not the name of one ancient country, people, ancestry, or language family. It is a geographic umbrella borrowed from modern linguistics for many non-Austronesian languages around New Guinea and neighboring islands. The imported shape is equally broad: ten disconnected components span highlands, rainforests, coasts, New Britain, Timor, Flores, Sumba, Maluku, and Sulawesi. Archaeology shows local histories, not a synchronized civilization. Highland gardeners managed wet ground; coastal settlements combined gardening, fishing, shellfish gathering, and pottery; island communities made tools and maintained changing exchange ties. Evidence differs sharply by place, and many dates are wide radiocarbon ranges. Houses, food remains, ditches, pottery, stone, shell, plant residues, and human remains answer different questions. They seldom reveal a person's language, family rules, lesson plan, remedy, or toilet. The eight periods below are reading windows inside one approximate map interval, not political reigns. No securely attributed writing survives from 200 to 100 BCE, so no modern language sample is substituted. At 100 BCE the software label ends; diverse communities, languages, and skills continued across the region.

periods.title: 200 to 188 BCE: read an umbrella, not a state
periods.summary: The exact id first appears in the 200 BCE snapshot as ten disconnected polygons. That geometry preserves an imported regional label, not surveyed borders, shared government, or proof that every resident spoke a non-Austronesian language. Archaeological and linguistic identities must stay local.

periods.title: 188 to 176 BCE: highland water follows local plans
periods.summary: Kuk's broadly dated Phase 4 channels overlap these centuries and show careful drainage of cultivated wet ground. The evidence belongs to one highland landscape. It demonstrates technical planning and work, but it does not map one crop, labor system, sewer, or political authority across the atlas shape.

periods.title: 176 to 164 BCE: southern coasts hold distinct settlements
periods.summary: Southern coastal evidence near this broad interval includes substantial settlements, shell-impressed pottery, tools, and far-reaching interaction in neighboring locations. Dates and assemblages vary by site. Neither pots nor genetic patterns automatically name a language, ancestry, ethnic group, or unified Papuan society.

periods.title: 164 to 152 BCE: exchange links places without uniting them
periods.summary: Pottery and shell trace long-lived movements across south-coast, plateau, and island networks. Movement could connect partners across long distances while communities remained different. Archaeologists can source some materials, but rarely identify every traveler, route, bargain, spoken language, or social rule.

periods.title: 152 to 140 BCE: island crafts keep separate histories
periods.summary: Raja Ampat pottery, Massim settlement sequences, and New Britain obsidian studies each reveal regional choices and connections. Their chronologies overlap only broadly. A pot style or stone source is valuable evidence, yet neither acts as an identity card for every person who made, carried, or used it.

periods.title: 140 to 128 BCE: health evidence stays personal and patchy
periods.summary: Plants, teeth, bones, residues, and food chemistry can illuminate parts of health, diet, or work, but exact-period human remains are scarce. Later south-coast comparisons show nearby communities could differ. This window therefore avoids inventing a region-wide disease list, healer role, or medical recipe.

periods.title: 128 to 114 BCE: many languages resist one family tree
periods.summary: Today's evidence distinguishes numerous language families and isolates, while contact has also produced shared regional features. Classifications still change as documentation improves. Archaeological layers contain no speech recordings, so this window teaches diversity and uncertainty rather than assigning modern language names to ancient pots, genes, or polygons.

periods.title: 114 to 100 BCE: a software seam is not a collapse
periods.summary: The exact papuan id disappears from the 100 BCE snapshot and remains absent at 1 BCE. No cited archaeological study reports a matching regional conquest, depopulation, or language extinction. The defensible ending is continuity: local communities and their changing lifeways passed beyond an editorial map boundary.

sections.title: Reading the map without collapsing people

items.text: The database has one exact record, papuan, dated approximately 200 to 100 BCE. Coverage finds one border feature and no finished card. Those facts identify the missing atlas entry. They do not turn a modern umbrella word into an ancient people's self-name.

The only feature is a ten-component MultiPolygon with 609 positions, stretching from Sulawesi and Timor through Maluku, New Guinea, and western New Britain. The parts share no direct TopoJSON arcs with another feature. Coordinates describe artwork in a dataset, not ancient land ownership.

Test points fall inside near Kuk, Tari, Goroka, Kainantu, Lae, lower Sepik, Fakfak, Wamena, Timika, Merauke, Kerema, Kupang, Flores, and Sumba. Other points, including Wewak, Madang, Milne Bay, Manus, New Ireland, and Bougainville, fall outside. This is display reach, not an ethnicity test.

The imported summary correctly calls Papuan a geographic grouping of non-Austronesian languages and denies one genetic relationship. Research now recognizes many families, isolates, and contact histories. Even that linguistic definition cannot prove what every community inside an archaeological polygon spoke two millennia ago.

Existing cards for Papuan Neolithic Farmers and later Papuans remain separate because their exact ids, dates, and map associations differ. This card neither extends the farmer label forward nor drags medieval and colonial evidence backward. Similar names are a reason to check identities, not merge them.

The polygon spans mountain basins, swamp margins, river lowlands, rainforests, dry islands, and long coastlines. No single settlement plan fits those settings. West New Guinea research especially warns that language, culture, movement, and environment form complicated local histories, with major areas still archaeologically under-studied.

At Kuk, channels and patterned fields preserve repeated work in wet ground around a broad date range that crosses this interval. They show people reshaping a particular highland landscape. They do not reveal a map-wide capital, king, village census, or permanent plan followed everywhere.

Caution Bay excavations recover postholes, graves, pottery, food remains, and changing settlement traces along the southern coast. These materials let archaeologists compare activities through time. A posthole can outline a structure, but it cannot politely introduce every resident or explain their kinship rules.

Andarewa Cave in West Papua holds a long local sequence, yet preservation and excavation limits matter. Cave use cannot stand for open villages, gardens, or islands across the region. Archaeologists build histories layer by layer, and an empty square may mean erosion or sampling rather than nobody living nearby.

Massim island excavations show settlement and material traditions diversifying over long spans. Researchers connect those local foundations cautiously to later exchange histories. The evidence supports island communities with their own trajectories; it does not license copying the historic Kula system, household forms, or titles into 200 BCE.

Kuk's wetland channels show gardeners controlling excess water, while the preserved crop evidence for this particular phase remains limited. Older New Guinea agriculture included vegetatively propagated plants, but exact field contents could change. The safest picture is skilled local cultivation, not one menu served across ten polygons.

Coastal settlements combined plant foods with fish, shellfish, and other marine resources in locally different proportions. Pottery and food remains can reveal storage, cooking, and discard, but many organic meals vanish. A shell midden records eating and disposal more readily than a recipe or favorite snack.

Isotopes from lowland West New Guinea skeletons can compare broad diet patterns among individuals. They cannot name a stew, identify who cooked it, or cover communities without sampled remains. This method is powerful precisely when its local dates, bodies, and ecological setting stay visible.

Microscopic starch and wear on a Kaironk Valley pestle link a specific stone implement with plant processing. That is an impressive scientific clue, though the tool's context must be dated carefully. Residue identifies worked materials more securely than a recipe, owner's language, or lesson taught to a child.

At the Emo site, new excavations and radiocarbon dates reassess old claims about early Gulf pottery, sago, and the ancestry of later hiri exchange. The lesson is useful: re-dating can revise a famous story. Fully documented historic trade details should not be dropped unchanged into this interval.

Wañelek pottery, axes, and slate tools show that highland crafts and inland-coastal connections had deep foundations before 200 BCE. Some pottery was locally made. That finding complicates simple stories of outside packages arriving whole, while still leaving open who moved, what language they spoke, and why objects traveled.

Raja Ampat vessels made between roughly 3500 and 1000 years ago bracket the card's interval and reveal changing western-island potting traditions. Shapes and fabrics help trace practice and contact. They are not passports: one style cannot prove one ancestry, language, polity, or unchanging group of makers.

Obsidian from the Willaumez Peninsula can be matched to geological sources, turning tiny flakes into evidence for movement and exchange. Volcanic layers also date disruptions and recovery. The network was regional and changeable; it did not require one ruler, border office, or ten-component Papuan administration.

Giligilina preserves a small, layered pottery assemblage from centuries before this card. Its dates and shared motifs support seafaring connections along the south coast while leaving many questions open. Similar decoration can trace interaction more readily than it can prove one ethnicity, language, fixed market, or permanent alliance.

Decorated pottery from Kayu Batu is studied by a Papuan archaeologist who openly identifies chronological gaps. That honesty is part of good discovery. A beautiful design invites questions about skill and community, yet without secure dating it cannot decorate this exact century merely because it looks relevant.

Postholes, hearth areas, burials, and food debris can place people around structures, but they rarely label a nuclear family, clan, marriage rule, or gendered task. Later local studies also show family terms changing through history. The card therefore refuses one timeless kinship model across the region.

Oral traditions about later hiri relationships emphasize reciprocal partners and challenge portrayals of Gulf villagers as passive recipients. They restore Indigenous agency to exchange history. Because the accounts concern later remembered systems, this card uses their method and warning, not their named roles as a script for 200 BCE.

John Waiko's Binandere history shows how particular oral genres and generations can carry local knowledge while responding to colonial pressure. It is one people's scholarship, not a template for everyone called Papuan. Ancient social life should likewise be approached through named places and communities whenever evidence permits.

Community-centered archaeology in Papua New Guinea asks researchers to respect kastom, local exchange protocols, oral knowledge, and benefits for living communities. That changes how evidence is gathered and explained. It also cautions against treating ancestors as anonymous specimens or a huge polygon as a convenient single society.

Marine shell found far inland at Walufeni Cave suggests connections across ecological distance and research conducted with Papua New Guinea partners. A shell cannot identify every hand it passed through, but it can open careful questions about visits, gifts, exchange, memory, and relationships between coast and plateau.

No exact-period schoolroom or written curriculum is known. Children could learn the demanding skills visible in gardens, boats, toolmaking, food preparation, and language only through social life, but archaeology seldom preserves who taught whom. The card therefore names required knowledge without inventing ages, classrooms, examinations, or universal roles.

A modern Papua New Guinea education project records children learning Alekano, bilum making, traps, tools, and house-building from community instructors. It shows how guided participation can work today, not how every ancient lesson worked. Its value here is continuity of community-led teaching and a warning against back-projection.

Language documentation in the Morehead region finds neighboring languages tied to particular villages and different subgroups. Children learning a local language enter a fine-grained social world, not a continent-sized Papuan tongue. Today's locations cannot be projected backward, but they make the atlas umbrella's scale problem easy to see.

PNG National Research Institute writers describe language shift and the importance of learning Indigenous languages across generations. That is a present challenge faced by living communities. It does not reveal the words spoken in 150 BCE, yet it explains why modern language work belongs in the card's continuity story.

Toare community members and cultural institutions now document songs, dance, mask making, materials, and ancestral meanings. Their project shows heritage taught through practice and performance. These living forms are not unchanged fossils from the card's interval, so they illustrate community stewardship without supplying invented ancient costumes or ceremonies.

Exact-period health evidence is thin and uneven. Teeth and bones can record some stress, diet, injury, or disease, but soft-tissue illnesses and successful care may leave nothing. A later south-coast comparison found differences between nearby groups, reinforcing why one regional Papuan health profile would be misleading.

The Aitape Skull's environmental reassessment shows how one rare human remain can prompt several explanations, including a possible tsunami death. Context, sediments, and dating matter. It is much older than this card and supports methodological humility, not a claim that target-period communities shared one hazard story or burial practice.

Plants certainly mattered for food, fiber, shelter, and probably care, but reviewed exact-period layers do not securely name a remedy or healer. Modern Indigenous botanical knowledge is rich and local. Respecting it means neither pretending it is timeless nor converting a recent preparation into an ancient prescription.

Settlement near coasts, rivers, forests, swamps, and volcanic zones created different opportunities and risks. Willaumez research connects eruptions with changing land use and exchange, while coastal studies record marine livelihoods. Neither source supports a single regional disease list; health depended on place, season, work, and individual history.

Archaeologists can compare childhood stress markers in teeth, but such markers rarely identify one cause or the care a child received. Later south-coast samples are method examples, not exact-period patients. The responsible answer to many medicine questions is specific uncertainty, which is more useful than a colorful invented cure.

Kuk's major channels moved water away from cultivated wet ground. They demonstrate measurement, digging, maintenance, and landscape knowledge. They were agricultural drainage, not evidence for drinking-water pipes, baths, household sewers, or public toilets. Similar-looking trenches can have very different jobs, so context decides the interpretation.

Coastal and island households needed fresh water, but the reviewed exact-period sources do not identify one regional well, storage rule, or purification method. Rain, streams, springs, and containers would vary by setting. This card refuses to turn reasonable possibilities into excavated facts without local evidence.

Shell, broken pottery, animal bone, ash, and plant remains often survive because people discarded them. Archaeologists study where rubbish accumulated to reconstruct activity and diet. A midden is valuable evidence, but it is not proof of municipal collection, a cleanliness rule, or everyone's daily disposal routine.

No securely identified toilet or latrine from 200 to 100 BCE appeared in the reviewed regional sources. That absence does not prove people lacked designated places or hygiene practices; organic installations and surface habits preserve poorly. It means the honest toilet section is short on fixtures and long on caution.

A channel may look like ancient plumbing to an eager time traveler, but Kuk's excavators read soil, slope, dates, and field layout before naming its purpose. The gentle joke has a serious point: drains can water gardens or remove field water without ever serving a bathroom.

Papuan is a cover term for non-Austronesian languages, not a single branch of one family tree. Modern research identifies many families and isolates, alongside Austronesian neighbors and long contact. The polygon therefore cannot be colored as one ancient language, and speech cannot be read directly from pottery or genes.

Boundaries between an isolate and a small language family can change when documentation or comparison improves. Central Solomon research offers another heterogeneous regional grouping whose relationships remain uncertain. Classification is careful hypothesis-building, not a box that freezes communities forever or supplies exact borders for 150 BCE.

Papuan and Oceanic languages coexist across Island Melanesia, where contact and several historical scenarios complicate easy maps. A shared word or grammatical feature may reflect inheritance, borrowing, or convergence. Linguists need regular patterns and local evidence; resemblance alone cannot unite every language inside the atlas shape.

Oral traditions carry history, values, place knowledge, and relationships through performance and teaching. PNG scholars and heritage workers emphasize community authority in interpreting them. A tradition recorded recently must be dated and located carefully; it is evidence with a transmission history, not a verbatim transcript from two thousand years ago.

Written-language sample: none securely attributable to this 200 to 100 BCE umbrella. A linguistic study places the first Motu orthography and school publication in 1877, vastly later and for one Austronesian language. Substituting Motu, Tok Pisin, or any modern Papuan language would falsely universalize the region.

The strongest achievements are distributed knowledge systems: highland water control, coastal food strategies, local pottery, stone and shell expertise, and exchange across difficult terrain and sea. None requires an empire to be impressive. Their diversity is the discovery, because it replaces one imaginary civilization with many skilled local histories.

Modern archaeology itself improves when Papuan researchers, museums, landholders, and communities shape questions and interpretation. Community-centered work challenges outsider stories that portrayed people as passive or timeless. That achievement belongs to living stewards and scholars; it should inform how ancient evidence is handled without projecting modern identities backward.

Much later, European powers divided eastern New Guinea among German, British, and then Australian administrations. Their records reflect colonial priorities and sometimes harmful language. These events began nearly two millennia after the card, but they disrupted communities and also shaped the archives through which outsiders later described Papuan lives.

Western New Guinea followed a different later path, including Dutch rule and the 1962 Netherlands-Indonesia agreement with United Nations administration. A state treaty records a transfer of authority, not every Indigenous perspective or consent. The atlas polygon must never blur those distinct colonial and postcolonial histories into one ending.

Papua New Guinea's Constitution honors ancestors, customary wisdom, community interdependence, diversity, and future generations. PNG researchers also seek return and local care of cultural objects removed during colonial eras. Living peoples are present-day rights holders and knowledge keepers, not remnants of a vanished atlas color.

ending.text: At 100 BCE the exact papuan feature disappears from the atlas, but no reviewed source identifies a matching conquest, collapse, depopulation, or extinction of languages. The map changes labels while locally different communities, gardens, settlements, exchange ties, oral knowledge, and family histories continue. Later colonial borders brought real disruption, yet living peoples remain stewards of their lands, languages, histories, and futures.
